mainTopic: How שותפין split a shared חצר with a wall, when a neighbor must help build a fence, and the גמרא's first reading of the word מחיצה
overview: This opening משנה of בבא בתרא teaches that when partners agree to divide a shared חצר, the wall goes in the middle. Its material, and so its thickness, follows local custom. Each partner gives up half the space the wall needs, so if it falls, both own the land and the stones. The same duty to share in building applies to a גינה where fencing is customary. In a בקעה where fencing is not customary, one who wants a wall builds it alone on his own land and marks it, and it stays his. If both neighbors agree, they build it on the middle line, mark both sides, and it belongs to both. The גמרא then starts by explaining the word מחיצה. Its first assumption is that it means a wall, and it supports this with a ברייתא about a breached vineyard partition that must be fenced again and again.

steps.title: Partners build the dividing wall in the middle, following local custom
steps.stepSummary: When שותפין decide to divide a shared חצר, the wall is built in the middle, out of whatever material is customary in that place.
steps.simpleTranslation: Partners who want to put up a divider in their shared courtyard build the wall in the middle. Wherever people normally build with rough stone, cut stone, small bricks, or large bricks, that is what they use. Everything follows the custom of the region.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה opens the מסכתא with a basic rule: shared courtyard, both partners want a divider, so the wall goes right down the middle, made of the locally customary material.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two things are set here. First, location: the wall sits in the middle, so neither partner loses more land than the other. Second, material: neither partner can insist on something cheaper or fancier, because local custom decides.
steps.confusionAlert: The four materials are not a menu that either partner may pick from. The wall is made of whichever one is normally used in that place.

phrases.english: Partners who wanted to make a partition in a courtyard
build the wall in the middle.
In a place where people are accustomed to build with
rough stone, cut stone, small bricks, or large bricks, they build with that;
everything follows the custom of the region.

steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partners dividing a חצר build the wall in the middle, using the locally customary material.

steps.title: How much land each partner gives for each kind of wall
steps.stepSummary: For each material, the משנה says how many טפחים of land each partner gives up. Because both gave land and materials, if the wall falls, the spot and the stones belong to both.
steps.simpleTranslation: For rough stone, each one gives three handbreadths. For cut stone, each gives two and a half. For small bricks, each gives two. For large bricks, each gives one and a half. Therefore, if the wall falls, the place and the stones belong to both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה works out the numbers: for each material, how much of his own land each partner gives up for the wall. Then it draws a conclusion about who owns the wall if it collapses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each number is one partner's half, so the full wall is double: 6, 5, 4, or 3 טפחים thick. Rough stone makes the thickest wall and large bricks the thinnest. Since each gave an equal share of land and stones, both own the fallen wall's space and stones equally.

keyTerms.meaning: Rough, uncut stone (makes the thickest wall)
A handbreadth, a unit of measure

steps.confusionAlert: The numbers are each partner's share, not the wall's full thickness. Double them to get the wall's width.
steps.whatToRemember: Shared land plus shared materials means shared ownership. If the wall falls, both partners split the space and the stones.

phrases.english: With rough stone, this one gives three handbreadths,
phrases.notes: "Gives" means he gives up that much of his own side of the courtyard for the wall to stand on.

phrases.english: and that one gives three handbreadths.
With cut stone, this one gives two and a half handbreadths
and that one gives two and a half handbreadths.
With small bricks, this one gives two handbreadths
and that one gives two handbreadths.
With large bricks, this one gives one and a half handbreadths
and that one gives one and a half handbreadths.
Therefore, if the wall fell,
the place and the stones belong to both of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the measurements behind 'build in the middle' for each customary material
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Each partner gives half the wall's thickness, so a fallen wall's space and stones belong to both.

steps.title: Garden versus open fields: when a neighbor must help build
steps.stepSummary: In a גינה where fencing is customary, the neighbor is required to take part. In a בקעה where fencing is not customary, he is not required.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true of a garden: where people usually fence, the neighbor is obligated. But in open fields, where people usually don't fence, the neighbor is not obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה extends the rule to other kinds of land. Whether a neighbor must join in building depends on whether fencing is the custom there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Custom again decides. A גינה is usually fenced, so one owner can force the other to share the job. A בקעה is usually left open, so one owner cannot force the other to pay for a wall.

keyTerms.meaning: They obligate, meaning the court forces him

phrases.english: And similarly with a garden, in a place where people are accustomed to fence,
they obligate him.
phrases.notes: "Him" is the neighbor who did not want the fence. He is made to share in building it.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בַּבִּקְעָה – מְקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִגְדּוֹר
phrases.english: But with open fields, in a place where people are accustomed not to fence,
they do not obligate him,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the courtyard rule to a garden and contrasts it with open fields
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where fencing is customary, the neighbor is required to take part. Where it is not, he is not required.

steps.title: Building a wall alone on your own land in the open fields
steps.stepSummary: In a בקעה, one who wants a wall pulls back into his own land, builds it alone, and marks the outer side, so if it falls, the land and stones are his.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if he wants, he pulls back into his own land and builds, and puts a mark on the outside. Therefore, if the wall falls, the place and the stones are his.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה continues the בקעה case: a person who still wants a wall may build one, but only on his own land and at his own cost. Step 5 then covers the case where both neighbors agree.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the neighbor gave nothing, the wall must stand entirely on the builder's side. The חזית on the outer face shows it is his. This is the mirror image of the courtyard case: there both own the fallen wall, and here only the builder does.

keyTerms.meaning: Pulls in, withdraws into his own area
A mark on the wall showing who owns it
On the outside, the side facing the neighbor

steps.whatToRemember: Who gave the land and materials decides who owns the wall. Shared in the חצר means both own it. Built alone in the בקעה means only the builder owns it.

phrases.english: rather, if he wants,
phrases.notes: "He" is now the one who wants the wall, not the neighbor from the line before.

phrases.english: he pulls back into his own land and builds,
and makes a mark on the outer side.
Therefore, if the wall fell,
the place and the stones are his.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִם רָצָה, כּוֹנֵס לְתוֹךְ שֶׁלּוֹ וּבוֹנֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the open-fields case with the option of building alone
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a בקעה, one who builds alone does so on his own land with a mark, and the fallen wall's space and stones are his alone.

steps.title: A wall built with both neighbors' agreement belongs to both
steps.stepSummary: In a בקעה, if both neighbors agree to build, the wall goes in the middle with a mark on each side, so if it falls, the place and stones belong to both.
steps.simpleTranslation: If they built it with the agreement of both of them, they build the wall in the middle and make a mark on each side. Therefore, if the wall falls, the place and the stones belong to both of them.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה finishes the בקעה case. It explains what happens when both neighbors want the wall, even though walls are not usual there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 4, one neighbor built alone on his own land and marked only the outer side, so everything was his. Here both agreed, so the wall goes on the line between them and is marked on both sides. Because both shared in it, both own the spot and the stones if it falls.

keyTerms.meaning: With the agreement of both of them
A mark on the face of the wall showing whose side it is
On this side and on that side

steps.whatToRemember: Who owns a fallen wall depends on how it was built: built by one neighbor alone on his own land, it is his; built by both on the middle line with marks on both sides, it belongs to both.

phrases.english: If they made it with the agreement of both of them
they build the wall in the middle
and make a mark on this side and on that side.
Therefore, if the wall falls
the place and the stones belong to both of them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts with step 4: there one neighbor built alone, here both agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wall built by mutual agreement in a בקעה goes in the middle, is marked on both sides, and belongs to both.

steps.title: The first assumption: מחיצה means a wall
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא opens by explaining the משנה's word מחיצה. Its first assumption is that it means a wall (גודא).
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: They assumed: what is the meaning of מחיצה? A wall.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins its discussion by defining the key word of the משנה. It is setting up a proof that comes in the next line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה began with partners who want to make a מחיצה (step 1). The גמרא first understands this word as a physical wall, גודא. The word סברוה tells us this is only the starting assumption.

keyTerms.meaning: The word used in the משנה; here assumed to mean a partition

steps.confusionAlert: סברוה means 'they assumed at first.' When the גמרא uses this word, the assumption is a starting point and may still be questioned later.

phrases.english: GEMARA: They assumed:
What is "mechitza"? A wall.
phrases.notes: This is the word from the very first line of the משנה, about partners who want to make a מחיצה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה to the גמרא, going back to the משנה's opening word.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The first understanding is that מחיצה in the משנה means a wall.

steps.title: Proof from a ברייתא about a breached vineyard partition
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its assumption with a ברייתא where מחיצה clearly means a wall: a vineyard partition that was breached must be rebuilt, again and again.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: A vineyard partition that was breached, he says to him: "Fence it." If it was breached again, he says to him: "Fence it."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to show that the word מחיצה is used for a wall. In that ברייתא, a broken vineyard מחיצה is something you fence, so it must be a wall.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא uses the phrase מחיצת הכרם for something that can be breached and must be rebuilt with fencing. That only makes sense if a מחיצה is a physical wall. This supports the assumption in step 6.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is taught in a ברייתא

phrases.english: As it is taught in a ברייתא:
A vineyard's partition that was breached
he says to him: "Fence it."
If it was breached again
he says to him: "Fence it."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a source to back up the assumption in step 6.
steps.raayaObject: That מחיצה means a physical wall (גודא).
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a breached vineyard partition, where the owner is told to fence it.
